record.paper_title: The True Prosoluble Completion of a Group: Examples and Open Problems
record.original_question: Profinite Grothendieck problem for groups: let Gamma and Delta be residually finite groups, and let psi: Gamma -> Delta be a homomorphism such that the induced map on profinite completions PF(psi): PF(Gamma) -> PF(Delta) is an isomorphism, where PF(G) is the completion of G with respect to all finite-index normal subgroups. How far can psi fail to be an isomorphism? In particular, beyond the known examples where psi is not an isomorphism, what structural or finiteness hypotheses on Gamma and Delta force psi itself to be an isomorphism?

evidence.quote: (i) Let Γ, ∆ be two residually finite groups and let ψ : Γ −→ ∆ be a homomorphism such that, at the profinite level, the corresponding homomorphism P F (ψ) : P F (Γ) −→ P F (∆) is an isomorphism. How far from an isomorphism can ψ be?

There are examples with ψ not an isomorphism and P F (ψ) an isomorphism, with Γ, ∆ finitely generated [PlaTa–86] and finitely presented [BriGr–04]. If P F (ψ) is an isomorphism, there are known sufficient conditions1 on Γ and ∆ for ψ to be an isomorphism.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $\Gamma$ and $\Delta$ be residually finite groups (so the canonical maps from each group to its profinite completion are injective). For a group $G$, let $\widehat{G}$ denote the profinite completion of $G$, i.e. the inverse limit of the finite quotients $G/N$ over all normal subgroups $N$ of finite index in $G$.

Suppose $\psi:\Gamma\to\Delta$ is a group homomorphism such that the induced continuous homomorphism $\widehat{\psi}:\widehat{\Gamma}\to\widehat{\Delta}$ is an isomorphism of profinite groups.

(a) Quantify how far $\psi$ itself can fail to be an isomorphism. In particular, exhibit or rule out examples (beyond known constructions in the finitely generated and finitely presented settings) in which $\psi$ is not an isomorphism.

(b) Identify natural structural or finiteness hypotheses on $\Gamma$ and $\Delta$ (for instance, restrictions on subgroup growth, geometric, cohomological, or representation-theoretic finiteness properties) that are sufficient to force $\psi$ to be an isomorphism whenever $\widehat{\psi}$ is.
artifact.status_search_result: Grothendieck's original question (must $\psi$ be an isomorphism when $\widehat{\psi}$ is?) has been answered negatively: Platonov–Tavgen (1986) gave finitely generated counterexamples, and Bridson–Grunewald (Annals 2004) produced finitely presented, residually finite counterexamples, with further constructions giving continuously many such pairs and examples involving hyperbolic groups (e.g., recent work on relatively hyperbolic Grothendieck pairs, 2025). However, the broader question of classifying how far $\psi$ can fail to be an isomorphism and identifying sharp sufficient conditions on $\Gamma,\Delta$ forcing $\psi$ to be an isomorphism remains an active area with only partial sufficient conditions known.

status_evidence.title: Grothendieck's problems concerning profinite completions and representations of groups
status_evidence.snippet: Bridson and Grunewald construct finitely presented, residually finite pairs P < Γ with P not isomorphic to Γ but with isomorphic profinite completions.
status_evidence.claim: Counterexamples exist in the finitely presented residually finite setting.

status_evidence.title: Relatively hyperbolic groups, Grothendieck pairs, and uncountable profinite ambiguity among fibre products
status_evidence.snippet: Recent (2025) construction of further Grothendieck pairs using relatively hyperbolic groups, showing ongoing research on the extent of failure.
status_evidence.claim: The problem of measuring the failure of ψ to be an isomorphism remains an active research direction.

status_evidence.title: Nilpotent completions of groups, Grothendieck pairs, and four problems of Baumslag
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses Grothendieck pairs and constructions producing many residually finite groups with isomorphic profinite completions.
status_evidence.claim: Sufficient conditions and obstructions are only partially understood.
